arXiv ID: 2602.12303
Title: Astrophysics Wrapped 2025: Year-in-Review of Every Astrophysics arXiv Paper from 2025
Authors: Rommulus Francis Lewis, Hetansh Shah, Amruth Alfred
Year: 2026
Abstract: Astrophysics has experienced an overwhelming increase in research output, as is evident from the year-over-year increase in the number of research papers submitted to the online repository arXiv. As a result, keeping up with progress happening outside our respective sub-fields can be exhausting. While it is impossible to be informed on every single aspect of every sub-field, this paper aims to be the next best thing. We present a summary of statistics for every paper uploaded onto the Astrophysics arXiv over the past year - 2025. We analyse a host of metrics like the most used keywords, subfields and telescopes, the distribution of journals, the most studied astrophysical objects like GW, GRB, FRB events, exoplanets and much more. We also indexed the authors' affiliations to put into context the global distribution of research and collaboration. Combining this data with the citation information of each paper allows us to understand how influential different papers have been on the progress of the field this year. We also present a first of its kind Astrophysical Spectral Fingerprint showing the distribution of research across the electromagnetic spectrum as well as the distribution of research by redshift. Overall, these statistics highlight the general current state of the field, the hot topics people are working on and the different research communities across the globe and how they function. We hope that this is helpful for both students and professionals alike to adapt their current trajectories to better benefit the field.

brief.summary: No source we found gives a direct count of 2025 arXiv papers on galaxy cluster physics, so this has to be built from a total and a fraction. My rough estimate is about 1,000 to 1,500 papers where clusters (the intracluster medium, cluster cosmology, cluster lensing, radio relics and halos, brightest cluster galaxies, cluster mergers) are the main subject, with a central value near 1,200. If 'on galaxy clusters' is read broadly, to include any paper where clusters are an important tool or sample (for example, galaxies in cluster environments or lensed high-redshift sources behind clusters), the count is more like 2,000 to 3,000. The total comes from a lead: a quote in a web search result (not read at the source) says the Open Journal of Astrophysics published 213 papers in 2025, 'only just over 1%' of astro-ph submissions. That puts new astro-ph submissions in 2025 at roughly 17,000 to 20,000, and around 20,000 to 25,000 if cross-lists from other archives are counted. As a cross-check, the AstroMLab 5 dataset contains 408,590 astro-ph papers from 1992 through July 2025, which fits a recent rate of roughly 18,000 to 20,000 or more per year. For the fraction, I assumed from general knowledge, not from any source found here, that cluster-focused work makes up about 5 to 8% of astro-ph. It sits mainly in astro-ph.CO and astro-ph.GA, with some in astro-ph.HE. So roughly 0.06 x 19,000 gives about 1,100, and the uncertainty is about a factor of 1.5. 'Astrophysics Wrapped 2025' (arXiv:2602.12303) analyses keywords and subfields for every 2025 astro-ph paper and may give a better fraction, but only its abstract was available.

issues.text: Step 1 counts a 'Gravitational Lensing' bar as cluster-related. Most lensing papers are weak/CMB lensing, galaxy-galaxy lensing or microlensing, so this would inflate the strict share. Record it only as an upper bound for the broad count, and never add it to cluster-specific keywords.

If the cited method text does not give both, report the figure-read value as a keyword frequency only. Do not use it to replace the assumed fraction. State in advance what happens then: the result stays assumption-driven, and the reconciliation must say so rather than present a refined central value.

The Table 7 CAS row (Galaxy Clusters as a top institutional keyword) is qualitative. It does not anchor a share and should not be presented as one. Cite it only as support that clusters are a major topic.

The reconciliation of f-003 and f-007 needs a decision rule fixed before reading the figures. List the per-category fractions each estimate assumed (CO, GA, HE, IM). Then state which ones the new anchor constrains, and update only those. Otherwise the final value risks being an unexplained midpoint.

The 2024 back-projection that assumes a constant share is circular. It just rescales 2025 by 1/1.142 and cannot check the 2025 figure. Label it as non-independent. It should not count toward the brief's year-on-year robustness item.

Budget is tight: figures, download, several chunk reads, 3 searches plus a second download, and several cite calls come close to 23. Move the generic bibliometric search after the AstroMLab 5 check (see added direction), or cap it at 2 searches.

2.METHODS
In this section, we outline how we collected our data and
the various metrics we utilise in the rest of this paper.
We also define some useful indices which we will reference
later on in our analysis.
2.1.Data
The data used in this analysis consists of all 18660 pa-
pers uploaded to the arXiv in 2025 under Astrophysics.
This does not include replacement submissions, as re-
placement submissions usually only involve changes in
paper content, which we do not collect. The dataset
also does not include cross-submissions, so as to confine
the dataset to only pure Astrophysics papers. Each of
these papers is assigned a Primary Subject by the au-
thor out of a list of seven categories - Astrophysics of
Galaxies, High Energy Astrophysical Phenomena, Solar
and Stellar Physics, Cosmology and Nongalactic Astro-
physics, Earth and Planetary Astrophysics, Instrumen-
tation and Methods for Astrophysics and a final general
category, Astrophysics. A submission also includes com-
ments where authors typically mention the number of
pages, tables and figures as well as publication informa-
tion. This metadata, along with the title and abstract
of each paper, was obtained by scraping the new submis-
sions of the arXiv everyday over the past year, a practice
which also enabled us to track the exact date a paper
was listed. We also utilise a series of other metrics which
are not inherently reported on the arXiv owing to which
we rely on other sources.
Citation information was collected using the NASA As-
trophysics Data System (NASA ADS 2), which tracks
both the total number of citations as well as the number
of citations excluding self-citations. While these metrics
are interesting in themselves, any statistics calculated
from them are sensitive to the fact that not all papers
on the arXiv are published in a journal. This is why
we develop our own citation indices to remove this bias
and highlight citation metrics specific to those papers
published in journals. We define the citation indices as
follows:
1. All Articles Citation (AAC): Under a certain cat-
egory, the AAC is defined as the average number
of citations for all articles under that category, in-
cluding articles that have not been published in a
journal. This number includes self-citations.
2. Journal Articles Citation (JAC): The JAC of a cat-
egory is the average number of citations per paper,
for papers under that category that are published
in a journal. We do not count arXiv e-prints as
journal papers, and hence citations to arXiv pa-
pers are not included in the JAC.
3. Excluding Self All Articles Citation (EAAC): The
same as the ACC, but only considering citation
count excluding self-citations.
4. Excluding Self Journal Articles Citation (EJAC):
Same as the JAC, but only considering citation
count excluding self-citations.
Although our analysis mainly focuses on AAC, we have
included extended statistics for all indices in Supplemen-
tary Information.
The calculation of citation indices requires us to flag
whether a paper has been published in a journal. How-
ever, considering how involved the act of publishing is
with the field we also thought it was necessary to track
which journal each paper was published in, information
that we use in our analysis of journals and journal costs.
To determine which journal a paper was published in, we
once again turned to NASA ADS, which filled in jour-
nal information for a substantial number of papers. We
note that this process was done in the third week of De-
cember (as late as possible) to allow sufficient time for
papers to go through the publication process. However,
it is not all encompassing and misses out on papers that
have been accepted for publication but are not yet pub-
lished. Thus, we turn to the arXiv comments left by au-
thors, which more often than not confirm a publication

2.3.Extracting Content-related Information
We did not want to limit this work to reporting number
statistics but instead wanted to reflect on the specific top-
ics and areas of interest that the community has focused
on. This required us to go beyond readily-available and
indexable metrics and look through the actual content
that papers are written about. Details like the telescope
used in a study or the sub-field referenced in a paper are
buried in the paper content. To extract these metrics, we
developed a general methodology of searching for words
and phrases related to the metric that are present in the
text of the title and abstract of a paper. The title and
abstract are the first two, if not only, sections of a pa-
per that a reader skims through before deciding if the
paper is interesting enough to warrant a proper perusal.
Knowing this, authors should only include the most rele-
vant and important pieces of information in the title and
abstract, which is why we believe it is justified to con-
duct our extraction only using these two sections of the
paper. As an added bonus, these sections do not per-
mit referencing, which limits authors to focus on their
work only, rather than prior literature, preventing our
extraction from picking up on referenced work.

2.4.Fidelity, Completeness and Caveats
Science must constantly wrestle with the fact that all
conclusions are subject to uncertainty. So is the case
with this paper. While we have the titles and abstracts
and basic metrics like citations for all papers and report
100% completeness, metrics which require more complex
extraction like the affiliations and content-related met-
rics, are subject to uncertainties. These uncertainties
are not in the form of incorrect information but rather in-
complete information. Since our extraction is strict and

with this paper. While we have the titles and abstracts
and basic metrics like citations for all papers and report
100% completeness, metrics which require more complex
extraction like the affiliations and content-related met-
rics, are subject to uncertainties. These uncertainties
are not in the form of incorrect information but rather in-
complete information. Since our extraction is strict and
is based on text taken directly from the arXiv, the possi-
bility of having errors or false positives is very low. Espe-
cially for the content related metrics, the search only trig-
ger if the search term is found. For a term like ‘JWST’,
there is only one subject this term could be referenced in
relation to. Thus, false positives are extremely rare.
We understand that this is not very convincing, which is
why we manually checked the accuracy and completeness
of these metrics for 100 randomly selected papers and re-
port fidelity metrics based on these papers. We find that
the most unreliable metrics are the pages, tables and
figures which, although 100% complete, are around 85%
accurate. This is only because of the fact that authors in-
consistently report these metrics inclusive or exclusive of
the appendix, in the arXiv comments. Nevertheless, this
does not affect any of the conclusions in this paper, and
the numbers differ by small numerical values. For cita-
tions, we report 100% completeness as NASA ADS keeps
track of preprint paper citations as well. Out of 100 pa-
pers, 97 of them had journal information complete and
correctly reported, with the three being incorrect only
due to the fact that our normalisation does not account
for very niche journal names. As for our content ex-
traction, we report 100% completeness and fidelity with
all papers having redshift-related phrases correctly ex-
tracted. We did, however, notice one paper with a tele-
scope mentioned that was not in our set list of searchable
telescopes, which is why our extraction missed it. Affil-
iations and geolocations are also well filled, with 96.4%
of papers having at least one extracted affiliation or ge-
olocation. Out of these, 95% of affiliations and locations
are correct, with the 5% of incorrect entries coming from
matching to country names associated with other sec-
tions of the paper, like the acknowledgements instead
of the affiliations. For the 96% of papers that we have
extracted affiliations for we report a 71% completeness
owing to extreme differences in LaTeX formatting. It is
important to keep in mind that this completeness is not
reflective of the number of affiliations missed on a pa-

of authors. Rather, its interpretation is 71% of papers
have at least 1 author affiliation missing. We note that
during our manual checking a vast majority of the time,
the code misses 1 or 2 author affiliations and rarely does
it completely fail on a paper. To put some form of a
number statistic to this, assuming on average an author
has only one affiliation (which is a reasonable assumption
considering having multiple affiliations on a single paper
is not very common), 97.8% of authors in our dataset
have an associated affiliation. All in all, our location and
affiliation statistics are near complete, given how difficult
it is to obtain a researcher’s affiliation, let alone extract
it from a set of non-conformal research papers.
A large language model approach for extracting metrics
was considered and tested, especially for affiliations, but
the cost involved for processing such a large dataset and
the possibility of hallucinations convinced us otherwise.
In fact, during a preliminary test, the LLM hallucinated
an author affiliation within the first five papers checked.
While this is presently unfeasible, with more experiment-

This uncertainty and incompleteness was not easy to deal
with since it almost always originates either from the fact
that a paper has a slightly different format that makes
it difficult to parse or from a search term that does not
cover the 0.1% of papers that include a rarely used niche
nomenclature. Hence, we must lay out some caveats.
The number statistics that we report are accurate and
precise, but do not have perfect precision. If we report
that a certain telescope has an ACC of 5.3, we expect

number. The focus should be more on comparing statis-

such inhomogeneous data. We also caveat this analysis
with the fact that parts of this paper use text match-
ing, which is sensitive to the terms we search for. These
search terms have been extensively constructed to ac-
count for diversity in writing and have aimed to be as
inclusive as possible. However, we cannot include every-
thing. We hope that the completeness statistics we re-

the effort to be inclusive and of the overwhelming major-

5.DISCUSSION
We have presented the most detailed and holistic
overview to date for all astrophysics research over the
past year in the form of papers uploaded to the arXiv

in 2025. We have explored these papers through a series
of different parameters and metrics to find and highlight
both number statistics as well as trends and patterns in
relation to the actual content in these papers.
Overall, the yearly increase in the number of research pa-
pers submitted to the arXiv is an indication that interest
in astrophysics is growing. The community is producing
papers at a rate of 52 articles a day. An astonishing 80%
of the papers uploaded to the arXiv end up being pub-
lished in a journal. These articles cover a diverse range of
subjects and utilise a variety of telescopes. We all work
in our small research groups or large collaborations on
both the hot topics and niche, ultra-specialised areas of
the field to produce papers that are journal-worthy most
of the time. We plan to include analysis across multiple
years once we have sufficient data, from past years as well
as the current year. This will provide a deeper insight
into any trends or patterns amongst the various metrics,
and enable predictions to be made for the future.
We believe the results in this paper can be useful for
predicting future trends and projecting statistics, which
could help better inform both students and profession-
als in their career planning as well as broader institutions
and collaboration teams on expectations for their respec-
tive sub-fields and areas of interest. It will also provide
a foundational basis for macro-decisions on the future of
astrophysics globally, such as informing the level of grant-
funding allocated to astrophysics research at the govern-
ment and university level, the proposal and construction
of new telescopes and observatories, and most impor-
tantly, informing critically, the direction of decadal sur-
veys like those carried out by NASA – to directly quote,
“NASA and its partners ask the National Research Coun-
cil once each decade to look out 10 or more years into
the future and prioritize research areas, observations, and
notional missions to make those observations” 3.
Our hope for this paper is that it shines light on the
different, and perhaps underappreciated, aspects of the
field and community, which in turn will promote healthy
collaboration between all scientists across the world and
open new avenues of research. It has been an amazing
year for Astrophysics, and we look forward to another
wonderful, ground-breaking year.

# How many arXiv papers on galaxy cluster physics appeared in 2025? A model-based estimate

## Abstract

No source located in this investigation gives a direct count of 2025 arXiv papers on galaxy cluster physics. The estimate is therefore built as a sourced total multiplied by assumed fractions.

The total is sourced. The year-in-review paper "Astrophysics Wrapped 2025" (arXiv:2602.12303) reports 18,660 astro-ph papers in 2025, counting primary submissions only, against 16,333 in 2024. It also gives counts for each subcategory.

The fractions are not sourced. Every within-category share of cluster papers used below is an assumption. No bibliometric source and no figure read could replace them.

On that basis, the reconciled estimates for 2025 are:

- **Strict count** (clusters as the main subject): about 920, range roughly 660 to 1,250.
- **Broad count** (clusters as an important tool or sample): about 1,640, range roughly 1,290 to 2,020, plus an unquantified number of cross-lists from gr-qc and hep-ph.

The uncertainty comes almost entirely from the assumed fractions, not from the total. The critic contested all three findings from this run, mainly because the central fractions are not anchored to data.

## Background

**The total count.** The key source is arXiv:2602.12303, "Astrophysics Wrapped 2025: Year-in-Review of Every Astrophysics arXiv Paper from 2025" (Lewis, Shah, Alfred). It compiles statistics on every 2025 astro-ph paper: keywords, subfields, telescopes, journals and geography.

Before this run, the total rested on an indirect lead. A web-search snippet, not read at the source, said the Open Journal of Astrophysics published 213 papers in 2025, "only just over 1%" of astro-ph submissions. That implies roughly 17,000 to 20,000 new astro-ph submissions, or about 20,000 to 25,000 including cross-lists.

**A second dataset.** AstroMLab 5 (arXiv:2511.12353) provides structured summaries and extracted concepts for 408,590 astro-ph papers from 1992 through

July 2025. This fits a recent rate of roughly 18,000 to 20,000 or more papers per year. Its concept tags were not accessed in this run.

**The fraction.** No paper found in the record reports what share of astro-ph is about galaxy clusters. The earlier working brief assumed, from general knowledge, a share of about 5 to 8%. That gave a strict central value near 1,200 and a broad range of 2,000 to 3,000.

**Earlier runs.** Two earlier runs on this thread produced conflicting strict estimates of about 1,200 and about 640. They differed mainly in the fractions assumed for astro-ph.CO and astro-ph.GA:

| Earlier estimate | CO share | GA share |
|---|---|---|
| About 1,200 | 15–25% | 8–12% |
| About 640 | 12% | 4% |

## Results

### The 2025 base count from arXiv:2602.12303

The full text of arXiv:2602.12303 was downloaded and read. It states that 18,660 research papers were published on arXiv under Astrophysics in 2025, compared with 16,333 in 2024. That is an average of 1,555 papers per month and year-on-year growth of 18,660/16,333 = 1.142, or +14.2%.

The board treats this base as primary submissions only, with no cross-lists. The open question of whether cross-lists are excluded has not been fully settled against arXiv's own statistics.

The subcategory counts used below are:

| Subcategory | 2025 papers |
|---|---|
| astro-ph.CO | 2,789 |
| astro-ph.GA | 4,761 |
| astro-ph.HE | 3,869 |
| astro-ph.IM | 1,722 |
| general astro-ph | 268 |

The 18,660 figure falls inside the 17,000 to 20,000 range inferred from the OJAp lead. That agreement supports the base.

### How the year-in-review assigns keywords and sub-fields

The methods text of arXiv:2602.12303, cited verbatim, explains the assignment:

- **Keywords.** 12,753 of the 18,660 papers (68%) carry author keywords. Each remaining paper is given three self-assigned keywords, chosen by matching common words in its title and abstract against a list of about 1,000 frequent author keywords.
- **Sub-fields.** These are a

ssigned one per paper, from a list of about 100 terms.

This has a practical consequence for any future figure read:

- A sub-field bar count in Fig. 13, divided by 18,660, would be a paper share directly.
- A keyword count in Fig. 12 cannot be converted that way, because papers carry a variable number of keywords (three or more).

### Figures 12 and 13 of arXiv:2602.12303 (extracted, not read)

Figure 12 ("Most Common Keywords for 2025") was extracted as two image files, fig12_1.png and fig12_2.png.

[[FIGURE 12]]

Figure 13 ("Top 25 sub-fields and research areas", based on paper titles and abstracts) was extracted as fig13.png.

[[FIGURE 13]]

These are the most direct 2025-specific sources for a cluster share. However, no tool available in this run could read pixel values. No bar values were read and none were guessed. Whether either figure contains a galaxy-cluster bar is unknown.

### Qualitative anchors from the paper's tables

Two tables give only qualitative information.

- **Table 8**, the top 25 author keywords (excluding self-assigned ones), contains no galaxy-cluster entry. It does include Cosmology, Dark Matter, Surveys, Hydrodynamics, Data Analysis and Interstellar Medium.
- **Table 7** lists "Galaxy Clusters" as the top keyword of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, with 7,837 author-weighted contributions.

These anchors constrain the share only weakly. The critic raised two problems:

- Cluster terms may be split across variants ("galaxy clusters", "clusters of galaxies", "intracluster medium"). That would keep any single variant out of the top 25 even if the combined share is substantial.
- The value of 7,837 for one keyword is large relative to an 18,660-paper base. Its definition should be checked before it is relied on even qualitatively.

### Reconciled 2025 estimate

All fractions below are assumptions applied to the sourced subcategory counts. astro-ph.SR and astro-ph.EP are set to zero, to exclude star, globular and open clusters.

**Strict est

imate (clusters as the main subject):**

| Category | Assumed share | Papers | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| CO | 15% | 2,789 | 418 |
| GA | 6% | 4,761 | 286 |
| HE | 4% | 3,869 | 155 |
| IM | 3% | 1,722 | 52 |
| general astro-ph | 3% | 268 | 8 |
| **Total** | | | **about 920** |

- Low end, with shares of 12/4/2.5/2/2%: 661.
- High end, with shares of 20/8/6/4/4%: 1,251.

**Broad estimate (clusters as an important tool or sample):**

| Category | Assumed share | Papers | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| CO | 25% | 2,789 | 697 |
| GA | 12% | 4,761 | 571 |
| HE | 7% | 3,869 | 271 |
| IM | 5% | 1,722 | 86 |
| general astro-ph | 5% | 268 | 13 |
| **Total** | | | **about 1,640** |

- Low end, with shares of 20/10/5/3/3%: about 1,290.
- High end, with shares of 30/15/9/6/6%: about 2,020.
- Cross-lists from gr-qc and hep-ph would add to this total but could not be quantified.

**Reconciling the earlier runs.** The about-1,200 estimate sits near the top of the strict range, and the about-640 estimate sits near the bottom. Two pieces of evidence were used to move the central value:

- The absence of "Galaxy Clusters" from Table 8 was taken to argue against GA shares of 8–12%.
- Its appearance as a top institutional keyword was taken to argue against a negligible share.

As noted above, the critic judged the first inference unvalidated. The chosen central fractions are therefore effectively midpoints, not data-constrained values.

**2024 back-projection.** Assuming a constant share and dividing by 1.142 gives about 800 to 805 strict papers and about 1,430 broad papers for 2024. This is a pure rescaling of the 2025 numbers. It is not an independent check and should not be read as evidence of robustness.

## Discussion

### What the run established

The main gain is a sourced and internally consistent base. It is 18,660 primary astro-ph papers in 2025 with a per-category breakdown, and it agrees with the indirect OJAp-based estimate of 17,000 to 20,000. With the base fi

xed, the final number depends almost entirely on how much of CO, GA and HE is assumed to be cluster work.

### Comparison with the earlier brief

The reconciled strict value of about 920 is lower than the earlier brief's central value of about 1,200 but overlaps its 1,000 to 1,500 range. The reconciled broad range of 1,290 to 2,020 is lower than the brief's 2,000 to 3,000 and touches it only at the top end.

The shift comes from smaller assumed fractions, not from new data. Both sets of numbers should be read as plausible orders of magnitude, about 10³ strict and about 1.5–2 × 10³ broad, not as measurements.

### Dead ends

A search for a citable bibliometric or topic-modelling study reporting a galaxy-cluster share of astro-ph found nothing usable. It consisted of three arXiv abstract searches (topic modelling of astro-ph, bibliometrics of subfields, LLM knowledge graphs of astronomy) and one web search.

- The closest lead was an LDA lead-lag study covering 1992–2011. It is too old and was found without an arXiv ID.
- arXiv:2406.01391, a knowledge graph on interdisciplinarity, gives no subfield shares in its abstract.

The planned figure read of Figs. 12 and 13 failed because no tool could read image pixels.

### Cautions raised by the critic during planning

- A "Gravitational Lensing" bar, if present, should not be counted toward the strict share. Most lensing papers are not about clusters, so it could serve at most as an upper bound for the broad count.
- Any keyword-frequency value would need the mean number of keywords per paper before it could replace an assumed fraction.

## Limitations

**The fractions are unmeasured.** Every within-category cluster share is an assumption. A factor-of-two difference in the CO and GA shares, which is roughly the spread between the two earlier runs, drives most of the uncertainty.

**No direct measurement was possible.** There was no ADS or arXiv API access for a keyword-facet count. The recommended query is abs:("galaxy clu

ster" OR "clusters of galaxies" OR intracluster) year:2025 collection:astronomy, with star clusters excluded. It was not run, and no hand sample was taken to measure the false-positive rate.

**The best figures went unread.** Figs. 12 and 13 of arXiv:2602.12303 were extracted but could not be read, so whether a cluster sub-field bar exists is unknown.

**Cross-lists are unquantified.** The cross-list contribution from gr-qc, hep-ph and physics to the broad count is not known. Whether the 18,660 base strictly excludes cross-lists has not been checked against arXiv's official monthly statistics.

**Several data issues remain open:**

- AstroMLab 5 concept tags were not examined.
- If they cover only January–July 2025, scaling to a full year raises seasonality questions.
- An all-years share may not represent 2025, given that eROSITA, Euclid and XRISM results were released that year.

**There is no year-on-year check.** No per-year cluster counts exist in the record. The 2024 figure is a non-independent rescaling.

**Borderline cases are unresolved.** It has not been decided how to count galaxy groups, cluster-scale simulations, and dark-matter or high-energy searches that use clusters only as targets.

**The run was budget-limited.** It used its single allotted wave.

## Open directions

1. Replace the assumed within-category fractions with a measured share by running the ADS abstract query for 2025 and hand-checking about 100 hits for star-cluster false positives.
2. Read Fig. 13 (and Fig. 12) of arXiv:2602.12303 with an OCR or pixel-reading tool, since any cluster sub-field bar divided by 18,660 would give a direct 2025 paper share.
3. Extract the galaxy-cluster concept share from the AstroMLab 5 tags (arXiv:2511.12353) for recent years as an independent anchor for the fraction.
4. Re-read the truncated passages of arXiv:2602.12303 to confirm the base and category counts verbatim and to check the definition of the 7,837 author-weighted contributions.
5. Obtain per-y

ear cluster counts for 2023 and 2024 from the same query, so the 2025 figure can be checked against a real trend instead of the +14.2% total-paper growth.
6. Bound the gr-qc and hep-ph cross-list contribution to the broad count, using arXiv's per-category statistics or the API.

As noted above, the critic judged the first inference unvalidated. The chosen central fractions are therefore effectively midpoints, not data-constrained values.

**2024 back-projection.** Assuming a constant share and dividing by 1.142 gives about 800 to 805 strict papers and about 1,430 broad papers for 2024. This is a pure rescaling of the 2025 numbers. It is not an independent check and should not be read as evidence of robustness.

## Discussion

### What the run established

The main gain is a sourced and internally consistent base. It is 18,660 primary astro-ph papers in 2025 with a per-category breakdown, and it agrees with the indirect OJAp-based estimate of 17,000 to 20,000. With the base fixed, the final number depends almost entirely on how much of CO, GA and HE is assumed to be cluster work.

### Comparison with the earlier brief

The reconciled strict value of about 920 is lower than the earlier brief's central value of about 1,200 but overlaps its 1,000 to 1,500 range. The reconciled broad range of 1,290 to 2,020 is lower than the brief's 2,000 to 3,000 and touches it only at the top end.

The shift comes from smaller assumed fractions, not from new data. Both sets of numbers should be read as plausible orders of magnitude, about 10³ strict and about 1.5–2 × 10³ broad, not as measurements.

### Dead ends

A search for a citable bibliometric or topic-modelling study reporting a galaxy-cluster share of astro-ph found nothing usable. It consisted of three arXiv abstract searches (topic modelling of astro-ph, bibliometrics of subfields, LLM knowledge graphs of astronomy) and one web search.

- The closest lead was an LDA lead-lag study covering 1992–2011. It is too old and was found without an arXiv ID.
- arXiv:2406.01391, a knowledge graph on interdisciplinarity, gives no subfield shares in its abstract.

The planned figure read of Figs. 12 and 13 failed because no tool could read image pixels.

### Cautions raised by the critic during planning

- A "Gravitational Lensing" bar, if present, should not be counted toward the strict share. Most lensing papers are not about clusters, so it could serve at most as an upper bound for the broad count.
- Any keyword-frequency value would need the mean number of keywords per paper before it could replace an assumed fraction.

## Limitations

**The fractions are unmeasured.** Every within-category cluster share is an assumption. A factor-of-two difference in the CO and GA shares, which is roughly the spread between the two earlier runs, drives most of the uncertainty.

**No direct measurement was possible.** There was no ADS or arXiv API access for a keyword-facet count. The recommended query is abs:("galaxy cluster" OR "clusters of galaxies" OR intracluster) year:2025 collection:astronomy, with star clusters excluded. It was not run, and no hand sample was taken to measure the false-positive rate.

**The best figures went unread.** Figs. 12 and 13 of arXiv:2602.12303 were extracted but could not be read, so whether a cluster sub-field bar exists is unknown.

**Cross-lists are unquantified.** The cross-list contribution from gr-qc, hep-ph and physics to the broad count is not known. Whether the 18,660 base strictly excludes cross-lists has not been checked against arXiv's official monthly statistics.

**Several data issues remain open:**

- AstroMLab 5 concept tags were not examined.
- If they cover only January–July 2025, scaling to a full year raises seasonality questions.
- An all-years share may not represent 2025, given that eROSITA, Euclid and XRISM results were released that year.

**There is no year-on-year check.** No per-year cluster counts exist in the record. The 2024 figure is a non-independent rescaling.

**Borderline cases are unresolved.** It has not been decided how to count galaxy groups, cluster-scale simulations, and dark-matter or high-energy searches that use clusters only as targets.

**The run was budget-limited.** It used its single allotted wave.

## Open directions

1. Replace the assumed within-category fractions with a measured share by running the ADS abstract query for 2025 and hand-checking about 100 hits for star-cluster false positives.
2. Read Fig. 13 (and Fig. 12) of arXiv:2602.12303 with an OCR or pixel-reading tool, since any cluster sub-field bar divided by 18,660 would give a direct 2025 paper share.
3. Extract the galaxy-cluster concept share from the AstroMLab 5 tags (arXiv:2511.12353) for recent years as an independent anchor for the fraction.
4. Re-read the truncated passages of arXiv:2602.12303 to confirm the base and category counts verbatim and to check the definition of the 7,837 author-weighted contributions.
5. Obtain per-year cluster counts for 2023 and 2024 from the same query, so the 2025 figure can be checked against a real trend instead of the +14.2% total-paper growth.
6. Bound the gr-qc and hep-ph cross-list contribution to the broad count, using arXiv's per-category statistics or the API.
